column4: Oftentimes in Christianity we think about repentance as fundamental only to the beginning of our faith in Jesus. The heart of repentance goes much deeper than turning away from sin unto salvation. Repentance from dead works means living with our hearts turned away from the things that harm us or stunt our growth-and turned toward the things of God.

column5: 3.  Preparation: Some steps have been taken toward change.

column4: 4.  Action: The behavior has been changed for a short time.
column5: 4.  Action: The behavior has been changed for some time.

column4: 5.  Maintenance: The behavior has been changed and continues to be maintained.
column5: 5.  Maintenance: The behavior has been changed and is being maintained.

column4: 1.  **Precontemplation**: He sees himself as a *firm* but *loving* parent. He believes raising his voice is necessary. He’s not considering changing. In fact, he might even justify it- “That’s how my dad raised me.”

column4: 2.  **Contemplation**: One day, after a long day at work, he snaps and yells at his young daughter harshly, louder and angrier than ever before. She flinches. Her lip trembles. She quietly walks away. In that moment… something **shifts**.

He will convict us of our actions and the state of our lives and hearts to open our eyes to see our complete and total need of Him.
column5: Although hitting rock bottom is more a myth than any definite precondition for change, God can still use sorrow to impress upon our minds. God will use sorrow to bring us to repentance. He will convict us about our actions and the state of our lives and hearts so that our eyes are opened and we see our total and complete need for Him.

column5: Godly sorrow, or the experience of such grief or distress that leads to a *metanoia*, is not the same as worldly sorrow. Worldly sorrow is the same experience of grief or distress, but the world offers no hope, only the promise of relief and death.

column4: Suffering is the endurance of pain-physical, emotional, mental, or spiritual-especially when prolonged or intense.

column4: Sorrow, suffering, and grief are closely related ideas. In the human condition we will experience all three, we can learn and grow through all three, but God will not bring about death and destruction in our lives to teach us.
column5: Sorrow, suffering, and grief are closely related ideas. In human life we will experience all three; we can learn and grow through them, but God will not bring death and destruction into our lives to teach us.

column4: A three-year-old boy was playing in the yard with his two-year-old sister. He was playing with a stick, and he intentionally hit her, causing her to cry and leaving a red mark.
column5: A three-year-old boy was playing in the yard with his two-year-old sister. He was playing with a stick, and he deliberately hit her with it, making her cry and leaving a red mark.

column4: Their father hearing the commotion investigated and when he learned what his son did took the stick, broke it in half and tossed it away. He sent his son inside to think about what did and comforted his daughter.
column5: Their father heard the noise and came to check, and when he found out what his son had done, he took the stick, broke it in half, and threw it away. He sent his son inside to reflect on what he had done and comforted his daughter.

column5: Godly sorrow and the goodness of God are interconnected. God is a good Father who will allow us to experience the consequences of our actions, yet will still stand with us as we go through those consequences.

column4: God's unrelenting goodness, to be willing to redeem us and restore us if we come to Him is a positive agent in our path of repentance. His goodness isn’t that we continue in sin, but that despite our sin He makes a way for us to be redeemed and experience His salvation.
column5: God’s steadfast goodness—that if we come to Him He is ready to deliver and restore us—is a positive factor on our path of repentance. His goodness is not that we remain in sin, but that in spite of our sin He makes a way for our deliverance and for us to experience His salvation.

column4: The Holy Spirit is the greatest agent for change mankind can engage with, and this is backed up by both the scriptures and by research. Research by “Lyons et al. column4: ### David’s Example of Repentance
column5: ### The Example of David’s Repentance

column4: Perhaps no account in the scriptures has a richer example of repentance than the story of King David’s sin found in 2 Samuel 11-12. It begins with King David remaining in Jerusalem instead of going to battle, where he sees Bathsheba bathing. Despite knowing she is the wife of Uriah, one of his loyal soldiers, David sends for her, and they have an affair, resulting in Bathsheba's pregnancy.
column5: Perhaps there is no richer example of repentance in Scripture than the story of King David’s sin described in 2 Samuel 11-12. It begins when King David remains in Jerusalem instead of going to war, where he sees Bathsheba bathing. Even knowing that she is the wife of Uriah, one of his loyal soldiers, David summons her, and they have relations, which leads to Bathsheba becoming pregnant.

column4: To cover his actions, David recalls Uriah from the battlefield, hoping he will spend time with Bathsheba and appear to be the child's father. However, Uriah, out of loyalty to his fellow soldiers, refuses to go to his home with Bethsheba. David then arranges for Uriah to be sent to the front lines where he is ultimately killed in battle. After Uriah's death, David hastily marries Bathsheba to cover up the pregnancy.
column5: To hide his act, David calls Uriah back from the battlefield, hoping that he will spend time with Bathsheba and appear to be the child’s father. But out of loyalty to his fellow soldiers, Uriah refuses to go to his home, to Bathsheba. Then David arranges for Uriah to be sent to the front, where he is ultimately killed in battle. After Uriah’s death, David hastily marries Bathsheba to conceal the pregnancy.

column4: The Lord is displeased with David's actions and sends the prophet Nathan to confront him. When confronted by the prophet, David immediately admitted, "*I have sinned against the Lord*" (2 Samuel 12:13). David did not try to justify or excuse his actions. This confession was the first step in his repentance, acknowledging his wrongdoing directly to God.
column5: The Lord was displeased with David’s actions and sent the prophet Nathan to rebuke him. When the prophet confronted him, David immediately admitted, “*I have sinned against the Lord*” (2 Samuel 12:13). David neither tried to justify his actions nor made excuses. This confession was the first step in his repentance, in which he acknowledged his offense directly before God.

column4: In Psalm 51, David’s words, “*For I know my transgressions, and my sin is always before me,*” show his complete ownership of his actions. He expresses grief not only for the sin itself but also for how it offended God, saying, “*Against you, you only, have I sinned.*” David displayed "*a broken and contrite heart,*" an essential part of true repentance (Psalms 51:17). This sorrow wasn’t superficial; he deeply grieved over the sin he committed and the hurt it caused. This depth of remorse was a sign that he wanted not only forgiveness but a changed heart.
column5: In Psalm 51 David’s words, “*For I know my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me,*” reflect full responsibility for his actions. He laments not only the sin but also that he has offended God, saying, “*Against you, you only, have I sinned.*” David showed a “*broken and contrite heart*”—an essential part of true repentance (Psalm 51:17). This grief was not superficial; he deeply lamented the sin he had committed and the hurt it caused. This profound remorse was a sign that he sought not merely forgiveness but a changed heart.

column4: David asked God to “*Create in me a pure heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me”* (Psalms 51:10). He sought an inner transformation that would prevent him from repeating the same mistakes. Rather than just apologizing, David pleaded with God to cleanse him, saying, “*Wash me, and I will be whiter than snow*” (Psalms 51:7). He recognized that only God could purify his heart and restore his joy.
column5: David prayed to God, “*Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me*” (Psalm 51:10). He asked for an inner transformation that would keep him from repeating the same mistakes. Rather than merely asking for forgiveness, David begged God to purify him, saying, “*Wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow*” (Psalm 51:7). He recognized that only God could cleanse his heart and restore his joy.

column4: David’s desire to be renewed spiritually reflects a genuine commitment to walk in God’s ways moving forward. His request for a “*willing spirit*” (Psalms 51:12) demonstrates his hope to be aligned with God in every part of his life.
column5: David’s desire to be spiritually renewed further reflects his genuine commitment to walk in God’s ways. His request for a “*willing spirit*” (Psalm 51:12) shows that he wanted to align with God in every part of his life.

column4: Although God put away David’s sin, the Lord struck the child and he was very sick. David fasted, prayed, and pleaded with God to spare the child, but when the child died, David accepted it (2 Samuel 12:15-23).
column5: Although God put away David’s sin, the Lord struck the child and he became very ill. David fasted, prayed, and pleaded with God for the child’s life, but when the child died, David accepted it (2 Samuel 12:15-23).

column4: In Psalm 51 we find a personal prayer of repentance and a public acknowledgment of his transgressions. David’s decision to write down his plea for mercy, creating one of the Bible’s most enduring psalms, shows his willingness to be transparent about his sin and God’s forgiveness. This psalm became a testimony of repentance and restoration for others to learn from, memorializing his journey from guilt to grace.
column5: In Psalm 51 we find a personal prayer of repentance and a public acknowledgment of his offenses. David’s decision to write his plea for mercy—which became one of the most enduring psalms in the Bible—shows his desire to be transparent about his sin and God’s forgiveness. This psalm became a testimony of repentance and restoration for others, memorializing his journey from guilt to grace.

column4: David’s repentance journey was not simply about feeling sorry; it was a profound change in his heart and life. Through confession, acceptance, and the heart transformation inscribed in Psalm 51, David memorialized his sin as a lesson on God’s mercy, repentance, and the possibility of restoration, making his story one of the Bible's most significant examples of genuine repentance.
column5: David’s journey of repentance was not merely about being sad; it was a deep transformation in his heart and life. Through confession, acceptance, and the heart-change inscribed in Psalm 51, David made his sin a lesson on God’s mercy, repentance, and the possibilities of restoration, making his story one of the most significant examples of true repentance in the Bible.
